draft_context.source_title: ‘A capable controller with plenty of adjustments’: while this Nintendo Switch 2 and PC gamepad looks like an Xbox controller, it hides some serious upgrades — but there are a few sticking points you need to know about
draft_context.description: Gulikit KK3 Max: One-minute review The GuliKit KK3 Max might look like a standard controller, but it has plenty of extras and features on board. Adopting the familiar form of the Xbox’s gamepad, the KK3 Max doesn’t exactly push the boundaries in terms of design. But given how comfortable and convenient the shape and layout are, it’s hard to complain about its lack of originality. There are also a few extra flourishes that add some interest. The matte white finish of my review unit was rather fetching, while the front panel is incredibly smooth, smoother than any other I’ve felt before. Its construction also feels quite solid, rivaling the builds of the best PC controllers . This premium feel extends to the buttons, since there’s very little wobble to any of them. The same can be said of the various sets of levers for the four back buttons, although a fair amount of force is required to insert them. (Image credit: Future) Despite the lack of software, there are still plenty of input-related customizations and settings available via various button combinations. These range from basic adjustments, such as the vibration intensity and stick sensitivity, to more advanced features, such as motion control and macro recording. The overall performance of the KK3 Max is pretty good. Most of the buttons are responsive and satisfying to press. The triggers offer a fair amount of control, although I found their travel distance a little too short for my preferences. The sticks also lack the precision of the best, although they move easily and quickly. Motion controls are also inconsistent: I found they performed well with Nintendo Switch games, but were less effective on PC and mobile titles. I’m happy to report that I had no issues with connectivity on any system I tried the KK3 Max with. Whether it was to my PC via the USB dongle or to my Switch and Android tablet via Bluetooth, the KK3 Max connected quickly to them all and I didn’t experience any dropouts or lag. Hotswitching between devices is also easy thanks to the dedicated button for this purpose, although it can take several presses for the button to respond. The current multiplatform controller market is certainly a competitive one, with an increasing number of entrants offering increasingly better value. At $79.99 / £65.99 / AU$113.95, the KK3 Max is dangerously close in price to some real standouts, such as the Steam Controller and the GameSir G7 Pro 8K , and more expensive than the 8BitDo Pro 3 , another highly capable controller. It mightn’t quite match up to its cohort, but the KK3 Max is still a gamepad to consider if you prefer onboard adjustments and like to have plenty of back buttons. (Image credit: Future) Gulikit KK3 Max review: Price & availability $79.99 / £65.99 / AU$113.95 Available now in various colorways Premium pricing puts it against big hitters The GuliKit KK3 Max costs $79.99 / £65.99 / AU$113.95 and is available now from Amazon. Three colorways are available: black, white, and grey. This pricing places the KK3 Max at the premium end of the market. It comes close to some big names in this space, such as the new Steam Controller . This has the advantage of touchpads for controlling the mouse cursor, and we found its gyroscope controls performed very well, unlike the KK3 Max’s. It isn’t compatible with the Switch or Switch 2, though. The KK3 Max is also more expensive than the 8BitDo Pro 3 , which has class-leading performance. We particularly loved its smooth analog sticks and triggers, as well as its phenomenal D-pad. It’s very customizable, too, thanks to its accompanying software — something the KK3 Max lacks. Gulikit KK3 Max review: Specs Gulikit KK3 Max Price $79.99 / £65.99 / AU$113.95 Weight 9.7oz / 275g Dimensions 6 x 4.3 x 1.3in / 154.7 x 108.1 x 32.4mm Compatibility PC, Switch, Switch 2, Android, iOS Connection type Wireless (2.4GHz, Bluetooth), Wired (USB-C) Battery life 15-28 hours (Image credit: Future) Gulikit KK3 Max review: Design and features Super smooth surface No extra D-pad hats or stick caps No software The KK3 Max has a simple and conventional design, replicating the form and layout of the best Xbox controllers . This is no bad thing, though, since such gamepads are among the most ergonomic and comfortable out there. Along with many others, I’m also particularly fond of the asymmetric analog sticks, since this moves the D-pad to a position that makes it easier to use with either thumb. What may prove more divisive, however, is the relatively small size of the entire unit. I don’t have particularly large hands, but both my thumbs and forefingers tended to overhang the sticks and triggers respectively. I was able to adjust my grip to compensate without sacrificing comfort or security, but others might find this more of a problem. There are some extra touches to the KK3 Max’s design that set it apart from the crowd. The brilliant white matte finish of my review unit is quite eye-catching, as is the subtle yet effective RGB lighting around the sticks, which also has a practical function that I’ll come to later. (Image credit: Future) The front plate is incredibly smooth to the touch, smoother than any other controller I’ve experienced. However, this plate isn’t magnetically attached as it is on other gamepads, allowing for easy removal for the sake of customization and reordering or replacing buttons. You can still remove the KK3 Max’s face buttons — you’ll just need to use the included puller to do so, which is thankfully easy to use. You can’t directly swap the X with the Y button or the A with the B, though, since they have different depths and curvatures. Rather, duplicates of each button are included in the box with the appropriate depth and curvature for swapping their position. This seems like a rather inefficient solution to me, and just means you have more bits of plastic in your life than you otherwise would. I can’t complain about their quality, though. They’re pleasantly smooth and stable, with only a marginal amount of play, while their transparent design is quite fetching. The D-pad also feels stable, although it’s a shame you can't replace the hat, as different designs can make a real difference to feel and performance, and would cater to more preferences. Fortunately, I found it quite ergonomic; even though it adopts the traditional four-point shape, its rounded edges make it better for rolling between directions. (Image credit: Future) The triggers are also comfortable. They have rounded outside edges, which makes them soft on the finger, as well as a dotted texture to provide grip. The analog stick caps are reasonably small but have an ergonomic shape and a soft finish. Their edges are slightly textured, although this is less prominent than other examples, so those with sweaty thumbs might slip off them. They are removable, but GuliKit doesn’t provide any extra sets in the box, which is a shame. The sticks themselves are quite tall and suitably planted, with a negligible amount of play. More solid are the back button levers. Despite how they look, they’re not made from metal, but they are reassuringly sturdy. They actually require a fair amount of force to insert in their slots, but once in place, I felt pretty confident that they weren’t going to come loose. They come in different shapes, with two sets of paddle-like levers and a set that looks more like bumpers. (Image credit: Future) There’s no software for customizing the inputs of the KK3 Max, which is a shame. However, there are still plenty of adjustments you can make and features to enable using various button combinations. You can alter the sensitivity of the analog sticks, with three levels to choose from, as well as toggle Dead Zone mode for them. You can also enable the Motion Aim Assist mode, letting you assign gyroscopic controls when either the left stick or the left trigger is held. Again, there are three levels of sensitivity to choose from here. Other settings include a toggle for the D-pad between four- and eight-direction modes, A and B and X and Y swaps, and a Rapid Trigger function with two modes to choose from: one where the chosen input triggers repeatedly when held, and the other when it’s merely pressed. An autopilot mode and a macro recorder are available, too. All these adjustments are quite easy to make, and there are some useful indicators that let you know what settings have been selected. For instance, the sticks light different colors depending on which of the three sensitivity levels is set, and the pad rumbles once, twice, or thrice depending on which of the three sensitivities of the Motion Aim Assist is set. However, I still would’ve preferred software for convenience's sake; it’s always nice to see your settings represented graphically, and having to remember all the button combinations is a hassle I could do without. (Image credit: Future) Gulikit KK3 Max review: Performance Solid button feel Slightly imprecise sticks Motion controls are mixed In action, the KK3 Max acquits itself rather well. The face buttons are tactile and well-damped, and only require a light touch to press, which makes them feel snappy. However, they don’t provide the best feedback, and there are times when it can be difficult to feel them actually being pressed. Thankfully, however, this didn’t result in presses failing to register, in my experience. The bumpers are more clicky, but still have enough dampening to make presses satisfying. However, I found their position a little too high, which can make reaching them a little difficult. I should say that I encounter this problem on quite a few gamepads, but here it’s particularly acute. In fact, I found the back buttons more usable than the bumpers, which isn’t something I can say about a lot of other controllers with back buttons. Their travel might be shallow, no matter which lever you decide to attach, but there’s enough dampening and feedback to make them viable as replacements for other inputs. I didn’t accidentally trigger them when gripping the KK3 Max tightly, either. The shapes of the various levers are easy to use, although I did find that the lower paddles were best used with two fingers rather than one. (Image credit: Future) The triggers are resistant enough to provide adequate control when performing graduated presses, something I especially appreciate when playing racing games such as Assetto Corsa that require precise acceleration and braking inputs. Their relatively shallow travel does negate this aspect somewhat, but I still found them just about up to the task. They’re also light enough to perform rapid inputs when needed, and to prevent fatigue from setting in during prolonged holds. The sticks move freely and quickly, with a fast rebound that makes them feel snappy. Aiming was quite accurate when I played 007 First Light , although they don’t offer the smoothest motion, with small but frequent jumps and unexpected accelerations affecting my accuracy. Thankfully, their aforementioned height didn’t pose a problem when moving them around, although it did cause some instability when pressing in the L3 and R3 buttons, with accidental directional movements often accompanying them. The gyroscopic motion controls are mixed in terms of their performance. When I played The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom on my Switch, they were smooth when aiming the bow, and on a par with the best Nintendo Switch controllers . However, with games on other platforms, such as First Light on PC and Hitman Blood Money — Reprisal on Android, they were jerky and restrictive in terms of movement. No matter how many times I recalibrated them using the onboard function to do this, they didn’t improve on these systems. I had no issues connecting the KK3 Max to my Windows 11 PC, Switch, or Android tablet via Bluetooth or the USB dongle. The handy button for hot-switching between devices is also useful, and hot-switching itself proved quick in my experience. However, the button doesn’t operate that well, taking a few too many presses to actually respond. Should I buy the Gulikit KK3 Max? Buy it if… You want a comfortable gamepad The ergonomic shape of the KK3 Max, combined with the super smooth front panel and rounded triggers, make it comfortable to use — although those with particularly large hands might struggle with it. You want plenty of back buttons With four back buttons and three different kinds of lever attachments for them, the KK3 Max is great for those who like to trigger inputs with their fingers rather than their thumbs. Don't buy it if… You want software Even though you can customize the inputs of the KK3 Max, you’ll need to do this with button combinations, as there’s no companion app. You want the best stick performance The sticks aren’t quite as smooth or precise as those in the best gamepads. Gulikit KK3 Max review: Also consider GuliKit KK3 Max 8BitDo Pro 3 Valve Steam Controller (2026) Price $79.99 / £65.99 / AU$113.95 $59.99 / £40 (around AU$84) $99 / £85 / AU$149 Weight 9.7oz / 275g 8.5oz / 242g 10.3oz / 292g Dimensions 6 x 4.3 x 1.3in / 154.7 x 108.1 x 32.4mm 6.1 x 3.9 x 2.6in / 154 x 101 x 65mm 4.4 x 6.3 x 2.2in / 111 x 159 x 57mm Compatibility PC, Switch, Switch 2, Android, iOS Switch, Switch 2, PC, Android, iOS PC, Mac, Android, iOS Connection type Wireless (2.4GHz, Bluetooth), Wired (USB-C) Wireless (2.4GHz, Bluetooth), Wired (USB-C) Steam Controller Puck, USB, Bluetooth Battery life 15-28 hours 15-20 hours 35+ hours Valve Steam Controller (2026) Valve’s latest iteration of the Steam Controller was highly anticipated, and in our view it didn’t disappoint. We found it offered great all-round performance, thanks to its TMR analog sticks and excellent gyro controls. Unlike other controllers, it also features touchpads for controlling cursor movement, making it a real boon for PC players. It doesn’t have the wide-ranging platform support of others, though. Read our full Valve Steam Controller (2026) review . 8BitDo Pro 3 If you want to spend less on a controller but still want great performance, look no further than the 8BitDo Pro 3. We loved the performance of its sticks, triggers, and D-pad, and we found its shape supremely comfortable, while still staying faithful to the old SNES gamepad it’s keen to emulate. It also has great software with plenty of customizations. Read our full 8BitDo Pro 3 review . (Image credit: Future) How I tested the Gulikit KK3 Max Tested consistently for a few days Played a variety of games on multiple devices Plenty of controller experience I tested the Gulikit KK3 Max for a few days, during which time I played a number of games on most of the platforms the controller is compatible with. I used it on my Windows 11 PC via the 2.4GHz wireless USB dongle, and on my Switch and Samsung Galaxy Tab S11 tablet via Bluetooth. I made sure to play a variety of games across these platforms to test every facet of the controller’s performance. I played 007 First Light on PC, which is a good test for the accuracy and precision of analog sticks, as well as Hitman: Blood Money — Reprisal on my tablet for the same purpose. I also played Assetto Corsa , which is not only a good test for the sticks but also for the control offered by the triggers. I also played The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom on Switch, primarily to test the motion controls, as the game and console handle such controls very well. I’ve been gaming for decades, and have used numerous gamepads with numerous systems in that time. I’ve also reviewed a number of other controllers, from budget offerings to high-performing premium models. Read more about how we test First reviewed: July 2026 ]]>

sections.body: Enterprise computer buying is currently going through an incredibly strange economic cycle. New PC shipment numbers from IDC show a divide across global deployment trends. On the one hand, actual device shipments are down nearly 5% across the industry. On the other side, overall manufacturer revenues are growing because prices are increasing across the board. Component shortages, driven largely by AI data centers (on top of worldwide government deficit spending), are consuming global memory allocations and resulting in major price increases across the industry. Yet, on top of this widespread industry downturn in shipments, Apple stands alone as the only major computer manufacturer posting shipment growth. Enterprise computer buying is currently going through an incredibly strange economic cycle. New PC shipment numbers from IDC show a divide across global deployment trends. On the one hand, actual device shipments are down nearly 5% across the industry. On the other side, overall manufacturer revenues are growing because prices are increasing across the board. Component shortages, driven largely by AI data centers (on top of worldwide government deficit spending), are consuming global memory allocations and resulting in major price increases across the industry. Yet, on top of this widespread industry downturn in shipments, Apple stands alone as the only major computer manufacturer posting shipment growth.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

“The real story here is the disconnect between units and dollars: shipments are falling, but revenue is climbing because vendors are pushing through price increases faster than demand is dropping,” said Jitesh Ubrani , research director for consumer devices at IDC. “Given worsening macro conditions and a memory shortage that isn’t expected to ease until early 2028, we don’t expect another round of inventory pull-forward, which points to a sharp slowdown in growth rates in the second half of 2026. Vendors are bracing for further price hikes into 2027, and channels are already flagging concern about elevated inventory at these higher price points.”

While enterprise vendors like HP, Dell, and Lenovo all experienced negative unit growth last quarter, Apple pulled a 10% spike in shipments. A quick glance at the market might lead you to believe this growth is only attributable to the MacBook Neo, but it’s more nuanced than that. In my opinion, Tim Cook’s greatest contribution to Apple is how well ran its supply chains are. Apple was one of the last manufacturers to raise its prices. Yes, the Neo is playing its part , but it’s definitely more than that.
What I am thinking about for enterprise buyers in the coming year boils down to Neo vs. Air. Said another way: lower cost on a shorter refresh cycle or a higher cost on a longer one?

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Ngày 6/8, Tạp chí Tài chính doanh nghiệp phối hợp Hội Tư vấn Thuế Việt Nam (VTCA) tổ chức hội thảo "Quản trị rủi ro thuế thương mại điện tử". Tác động thực tế nằm ở workflow, chi phí, rủi ro hoặc quyết định mua/dùng; Sàn TMĐT gửi sai doanh thu, hóa đơn của người bán cho cơ quan thuế: Ai sai - người đó chịu trách nhiệm nên được giải thích qua lăng kính đó trước khi kết luận rộng hơn. Phần này cần nối câu chuyện với workflow, chi phí, bảo mật hoặc quyết định dùng/mua của người đọc.

sections.heading: Chi tiết cần kiểm chứng
sections.body: Tại sự kiện, độc giả thắc mắc: Trong trường hợp người bán phát hiện doanh thu do sàn thương mại điện tử chuyển cho cơ quan thuế không khớp với doanh thu thực tế, người bán cần liên hệ với sàn hay cơ quan thuế để được xử lý? Quy trình điều chỉnh dữ liệu và trách nhiệm của từng bên được thực hiện như thế nào? Câu hỏi tiếp theo là tín hiệu này có thành rollout bền vững, thay đổi giá trị sản phẩm, giới hạn đáng chú ý hay chỉ là một nhịp cập nhật ngắn. Phần này chỉ giữ chi tiết có thể kiểm chứng và tránh lặp lại nguyên văn cách diễn đạt của nguồn.

sections.heading: Ai nên hành động hoặc chờ
sections.body: Ông Đặng Văn Thành, Phó Chi cục trưởng Chi cục Thuế Thương mại điện tử trả lời: Khi người bán phát hiện dữ liệu doanh thu do sàn thương mại điện tử chuyển đến cơ quan thuế không khớp với doanh thu thực tế, trước hết cần chủ động liên hệ với sàn thương mại điện tử để rà soát, đối chiếu và xác định nguyên nhân phát sinh sai lệch. Với người đọc, khung hữu ích gồm bằng chứng hiện có, nhóm bị ảnh hưởng, rủi ro còn lại và điểm nên kiểm tra trước khi hành động. Phần này cần gọi đúng nhóm độc giả nên hành động ngay hoặc nên chờ thêm xác nhận.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Trường hợp xác định có sai sót trong dữ liệu đã kê khai, sàn thương mại điện tử có trách nhiệm thực hiện kê khai bổ sung, điều chỉnh theo đúng quy định của pháp luật về quản lý thuế, đồng thời cập nhật lại thông tin đã gửi cho cơ quan thuế. Một bài tốt cần tách rõ sự kiện từ nguồn, tác động với người đọc và câu hỏi theo dõi để không giống bản tóm tắt link rời. Phần này nên khép lại bằng tín hiệu cần kiểm tra tiếp, không tóm tắt lại cùng một ý.

paragraphs: Người bán hàng trên sàn thương mại điện tử đang từng bước thích ứng với các quy định thuế mới. Ảnh minh họa từ Pexels.
Ngày 6/8, Tạp chí Tài chính doanh nghiệp phối hợp Hội Tư vấn Thuế Việt Nam (VTCA) tổ chức hội thảo "Quản trị rủi ro thuế thương mại điện tử".

Tại sự kiện, độc giả thắc mắc: Trong trường hợp người bán phát hiện doanh thu do sàn thương mại điện tử chuyển cho cơ quan thuế không khớp với doanh thu thực tế, người bán cần liên hệ với sàn hay cơ quan thuế để được xử lý? Trường hợp xác định có sai sót trong dữ liệu đã kê khai, sàn thương mại điện tử có trách nhiệm thực hiện kê khai bổ sung, điều chỉnh theo đúng quy định của pháp luật về quản lý thuế, đồng thời cập nhật lại thông tin đã gửi cho cơ quan thuế.

Về phía cơ quan thuế, việc tiếp nhận và cập nhật dữ liệu sẽ được thực hiện trên cơ sở hồ sơ điều chỉnh do sàn thương mại điện tử cung cấp. Vì vậy, người bán cần phối hợp chặt chẽ với sàn để bảo đảm thông tin doanh thu và nghĩa vụ thuế được cập nhật đầy đủ, chính xác.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì vừa đổi
sections.body: Bình luận mới được duyệt Xem tất cả Thông tin tài khoản Đổi mật khẩu Tin đã lưu Tin đã xem Đăng xuất Chính trị Chính trị Thời sự Thời sự Thế giới Thế giới Kinh tế Kinh tế Đời sống Đời sống Sức khỏe Sức khỏe Giới trẻ Giới trẻ Giáo dục Giáo dục Du lịch Du lịch Văn hóa Văn hóa Giải trí Giải trí Thể thao Thể thao Công nghệ Công nghệ - Game Xe Xe Video Video Tiêu dùng Tiêu dùng Thời trang trẻ Thời trang trẻ Đóng menu Chào ngày mới Tin 24h Tin thị trường Tin 360 Video Magazine Tiện ích Bạn cần biết Liên hệ Thông tin toà soạn Liên hệ quảng cáo Công nghệ Tin tức công nghệ Google Drive sắp ngừng tính năng sao lưu hình ảnh Phong Đỗ 08/08/2026 14:50 GMT+7 Chia sẻ Chọn Báo Thanh Niên làm nguồn ưu tiên trên Google tìm kiếm. Xem hướng dẫn. BƯỚC 1 Nhấp vào nút "Thêm Thanh Niên trên Google" hoặc mở trực tiếp đường dẫn này: https://www. google. com/preferences/source? q=thanhnien. vn BƯỚC 2 Tại trang vừa mở, tìm dòng "Báo Thanh Niên " và bấm vào ô vuông bên phải. Khi ô vuông chuyển thành dấu tích xanh là bạn đã thành công rồi! LƯU Ý NHỎ: Nếu muốn kiểm tra xem cài đặt còn hiệu lực không, bạn chỉ cần mở lại link trên là thấy ngay dấu tích xanh vẫn đang hiển thị. Chúc bạn đọc báo vui vẻ! --> Google Drive chuẩn bị thay đổi chính sách sao lưu hình ảnh, người dùng cần lưu ý để tránh mất tiền oan. Google vừa phát đi thông báo quan trọng về việc chấm dứt hỗ trợ đồng bộ tự động giữa bản sao lưu Google Drive trên máy tính và Google Photos. Thời hạn chính thức áp dụng thay đổi này là từ ngày 10. 8. 2026. Nếu đang phụ thuộc vào Drive để sao lưu ảnh từ máy tính, người dùng sẽ bắt buộc phải tìm giải pháp thay thế. Sau mốc thời gian này, việc tải hình ảnh lên Google Photos sẽ thay đổi hoàn toàn. Tín hiệu từ Thanh Nien Cong Nghe cần được đặt vào bối cảnh trước: thời điểm xuất hiện, chi tiết đã có cơ sở và lý do nó đáng nằm trong dòng tin công nghệ hôm nay. Phần này cần dựng lại thay đổi đã có cơ sở trước khi chuyển sang nhận định.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Để tiếp tục sao lưu trên máy tính, người dùng cần truy cập phiên bản web của Google Photos, bấm biểu tượng '+' > chọn mục 'Back up folders' (Sao lưu thư mục) và trỏ tới thư mục hình trên máy tính muốn sao lưu lên đám mây. Tác động thực tế nằm ở workflow, chi phí, rủi ro hoặc quyết định mua/dùng; Google Drive sắp ngừng tính năng sao lưu hình ảnh nên được giải thích qua lăng kính đó trước khi kết luận rộng hơn. Phần này cần nối câu chuyện với workflow, chi phí, bảo mật hoặc quyết định dùng/mua của người đọc.

sections.heading: Chi tiết cần kiểm chứng
sections.body: Những hình ảnh đã tải lên Google Drive trước mốc 10. 8 vẫn sẽ được giữ nguyên vẹn và an toàn. Tuy nhiên, các ảnh mới tải lên Drive sau thời điểm này sẽ không còn tự động chuyển sang Google Photos. Để tránh lãng phí dung lượng bộ nhớ không cần thiết, người dùng nên chủ động tắt tính năng sao lưu thư mục ảnh trên Drive. Điều này giúp bạn tránh nguy cơ phải mua thêm các gói dung lượng Google One không thực sự cần thiết. Câu hỏi tiếp theo là tín hiệu này có thành rollout bền vững, thay đổi giá trị sản phẩm, giới hạn đáng chú ý hay chỉ là một nhịp cập nhật ngắn. Phần này chỉ giữ chi tiết có thể kiểm chứng và tránh lặp lại nguyên văn cách diễn đạt của nguồn.

sections.heading: Ai nên hành động hoặc chờ
sections.body: Bạn cũng có thể kiểm tra nguồn gốc tải lên của từng tấm hình bằng biểu tượng thông tin (File information) trên giao diện web. Việc chủ động quản lý thư mục giúp bạn tối ưu hóa không gian lưu trữ cá nhân hiệu quả hơn. Với người đọc, khung hữu ích gồm bằng chứng hiện có, nhóm bị ảnh hưởng, rủi ro còn lại và điểm nên kiểm tra trước khi hành động. Phần này cần gọi đúng nhóm độc giả nên hành động ngay hoặc nên chờ thêm xác nhận.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Sự thay đổi chính sách này ảnh hưởng nhiều nhất đến những người dùng máy ảnh chuyên dụng hoặc có thư viện ảnh cũ. Với ảnh chụp từ điện thoại Android hay iPhone, dữ liệu thường đã được lưu sẵn qua các ứng dụng di động tương ứng. Dù vậy, người dùng vẫn nên tạo thêm các bản sao lưu dự phòng trên ổ cứng ngoài hoặc dịch vụ đám mây khác. Thói quen này giúp bảo vệ an toàn cho kho hình ảnh cá nhân, tránh rủi ro mất mát dữ liệu không đáng có. Một bài tốt cần tách rõ sự kiện từ nguồn, tác động với người đọc và câu hỏi theo dõi để không giống bản tóm tắt link rời. Phần này nên khép lại bằng tín hiệu cần kiểm tra tiếp, không tóm tắt lại cùng một ý.

Thói quen này giúp bảo vệ an toàn cho kho hình ảnh cá nhân, tránh rủi ro mất mát dữ liệu không đáng có.

draft_context.source_title: Unveiling good and bad behaviors on the Agentic Internet
draft_context.description: The Internet isn’t a single lane of traffic. For a long time, the rule of thumb in web security was that bots are bad, while humans are good. Of course, we’re far past this generalization. Humans can be fraudulent, and bots can be helpful at different levels. Site owners actively want some automated traffic to interact with our sites to make the Internet functional and discoverable. To complicate things further, the line between "human" and "bot" is blurring more and more. Now, we have a type of “hybrid” traffic where a single session shifts from human to agentic and back again. (Think of a user browsing a store, and then handing off the checkout process to an automated shopping assistant.) So, how do website owners manage this kind of complexity? What matters here is assessing behaviors . Is this behavior abusive? Malicious? What’s the risk presented here, and can I trust this visitor based on their actions? Solving this requires moving beyond static, point-in-time checks. It requires analyzing continuous behaviors to evaluate Trust. In this post, we’ll share an inside look into the strategy of the Web Integrity & Trust team (covering the bots and fraud problem spaces) around detecting and analyzing good and bad behaviors, providing tools to help site owners tackle emerging challenges in the shifting Agentic Internet. We’ll also share findings around agentic traffic since the launch of Precursor , and a simulation where you can see how your own cursor movements would be assessed as human or bot — plus some exciting launch updates to expect in the near future. Defining Risk and Trust Let’s talk about the distinction between Risk and Trust , the way we discuss it within the teams at Cloudflare who work in bot detection. These are often viewed as polar opposites of a continuum. At Cloudflare, we look at them as independent, but reciprocal, values. Trust is the essential ingredient in making informed decisions on what to do about your traffic. Risk is how likely something like a request or action is to be harmful, and it’s often ephemeral. Trust, however, is built up over time, and it’s based on reputation. We can illustrate this with an example from real life: say that you’re enjoying some evening television at home, when suddenly, you hear the doorbell being rung repeatedly. Besides being annoying, this behavior is strange. Frantic doorbell rings late at night are alarming. You check through your door camera and see that the person ringing your doorbell is your best friend who lives next door. Of course, you trust your best friend, and we’d bet you would let them in. In this example, it wouldn’t be enough for you to say, “Reject anyone who rings my doorbell at night” or “Reject anyone who rings my doorbell more than 10 times.” Again, Trust is the essential ingredient. Going back to traffic on the Internet, the strategy as we build products in the bots and fraud space focuses on building an entire ecosystem based on Trust. And our goal is to provide the incentives and primitives for site owners to use to incentivize behavior that makes the Internet safer for everyone: starting with blocking malicious activity at the bottom, to encouraging participation in a safer Internet at the top. Good behaviors, rooted in transparency Starting at the top: what counts as good behavior? We can draw clear examples from the Verified bots and agents within BotBase. Last month, we announced an updated pragmatic taxonomy for the good bots we track in our system , boiling down the definition of “ Verified ” to two things: 1) you declare yourself honestly, and 2) you don’t abuse the trust you’ve earned. Transparency between a site owner and a bot operator allows for a symbiotic relationship: site owners can note what behaviors and data uses they want to allow on their websites, and bot operators can be granted access more easily. The transparency allows for Trust in the relationship; if you have nothing to hide, declaring who you are should reduce friction from the sites who want to allow your behaviors. BotBase is not meant to only make declarations of “who is good”. It is intended to be a directory of all known bots and agents, and provide the facts. Compared to our previous Bots Directory, which only included known good bots, BotBase is also capable of tracking less-than-good bots and agents. Why? Because our systems track and validate behavior for known good actors, meaning we have the tools to identify when these expectations aren’t met. If you abuse trust on the Cloudflare network, you should not be easily allowed, so you will be unverified. Bad behaviors: blatant, stealthy, and everything in between A few weeks ago, we announced Precursor , a continuous client-side system to detect even subtly inhuman bot traffic that can fly under the radar when assessing network signals alone. When a customer enables Precursor, the JavaScript detection is CDN-injected, so it doesn’t require sitting at the computer and figuring out where or how to rerun these detections. What's more, Precursor evaluates user behavior continuously throughout the session , so no more free hall passes for abusive traffic that found a way to pass client and browser-side checks just once. Applying our Risk and Trust framework to these client-side detections, we can point out that CAPTCHAs or one-time hurdles are Risk-based, meaning they lack context . On the other hand, verification using behavioral tells is Trust-based, since it can capture more context clues from the full user session. Precursor is the tool for us to analyze this behavior. To sum it up, Precursor is so powerful because it: Provides Trust-based detection over the entire user session. Drives up the cost for bot developers to replicate human behavior over a multipage timeline. By making it economically disadvantageous for bot developers to outrun these detections, we win the adversarial game. Now, what have we learned since we’ve launched? Looking at just a 24-hour period at the time of writing this blog, we can see 206 million Precursor evaluation events , across 73,438 zones on the Cloudflare network. We can see patterns in the data that reveal things that we had suspected when launching the detection, but can now validate across tens of thousands of domains: Suspicious behavior often happens mid-session, which point-in-time detection wouldn’t catch. Behavior often shifts from human to agentic and back over a session . In these cases, it’s important to understand the intent so that site owners don’t block user flows that they actually want. This highlights the importance of a bot classification system that allows website owners to handle traffic by use case, purpose, and data use. This is precisely why we prioritized taxonomy updates for BotBase. For those curious to learn more on how Precursor actually works, we shared a sneak peek — how the signals we analyze showed us that to err is human — in our announcement blog post . Today, we’re going a step further: giving anyone on the Internet an interactive demo simulating how Precursor would trace your cursor movements. Precursor Trace is live now, sharing how we’d assess your cursor movements using (part of) Precursor’s detection mechanism. Here, you can see whether you’re accelerating or correcting yourself, the rhythm and texture of your cursor movement, and more — all things you’ve probably never thought about as a real human being interacting with a computer. Try it out! Adaptive Intelligence is coming soon Cloudflare’s bot detection engines can produce different outcomes when assessing if a given request is automated or not. For requests that are deemed to be automated, the assessment can be 1) definitely automated, based on proven, deterministic methods or fingerprints of bots, or 2) likely automated, based on predictive scoring from Cloudflare’s Bots ML. Historically, Bots ML has been updated in versions, meaning we announced each new model version as a product launch. This pacing doesn’t work when bots adapt on the scale of hours or even minutes. Adaptive Intelligence, a completely new detection engine, is different from anything we’ve built before in the Bots ML space. The model itself is adaptive . It has learned from everything we’ve seen in the past, but more importantly, it will continue to learn and self-adjust based on what it sees. Adaptive Intelligence will upgrade itself based on a wide range of traffic patterns we identify, from good to bad behaviors, and customers will no longer need to upgrade to a formal new model version to have the latest predictive bot detections working for them. All Bot Management customers will have access to Adaptive Intelligence in the near future — stay tuned for the launch announcement coming soon. Moving beyond determinism to influence bot behavior So far, we’ve focused on Cloudflare’s side of things: strategy, detection, and taxonomy. All of this allows Cloudflare to equip website owners with the tools they need to set the traffic policies they want on their sites. Zooming in on the website owner side, we want to take this chance to discuss some advanced mitigations that allow website owners themselves to influence bot behavior. With more blatant mitigation techniques, we face something that we’ve nicknamed the “Bot Antibiotic Problem.” Always sending bots a deterministic response (like a 403 block) makes it easy for a malicious developer bot to probe, observe, and reverse-engineer your defenses. We know this, so we’re designing mitigations specifically made for throttling bots — with different approaches for malicious bots vs. benign bots. We can break them down into three approaches: Approach 1: Unpredictability and Random Actions. Applying random responses (between block, challenge, or allow) to suspected automated traffic breaks a bot's automated retry logic and fingerprinting. Approach 2: AI Labyrinth , a defensive response that traps unauthorized bots in an endless maze of AI-generated web pages. You can waste malicious bots' compute and crawl budgets by using misdirection . Site owners will be given three options within AI Labyrinth, depending on their preference: Maze : Generates an endless web of linked pages for bots to follow. Summary : Feeds crawlers an LLM-generated summary of a page that looks real but is entirely useless as AI training data. Poison : Serves deliberately fake content (like fake prices or inventory) to a bot, polluting the data it collects for AI training. Approach 3: Queuing for Good Bots. Not all agentic traffic is bad; queuing manages throughput for legitimate automated traffic (like user-directed shopping agents) without denying them service entirely. These advanced, bot-specific mitigations are set to roll out closer towards the end of the year, and will be available for the website owner to choose how strict they want their mitigations to be. We also know that a great defense is a predictive one — one that self-learns and course-corrects without needing multiple security experts on a call to reactively set a fix that accounts for the latest stealth attack. This might look like having a system of “disposable” rules, in which the ruleset is dynamic in nature. This is by design: if attacks constantly evolve, the defenses should, too. That’s why we’re working to keep both detections and mitigations a step ahead. Establish the Trust ecosystem that works for you Anyone and everyone can take steps to define how automated agents interact with their infrastructure. A few things to try: Turn on Precursor Play around with Precursor Trace Explore BotBase By moving away from static, point-in-time checks and embracing continuous trust evaluation, we reduce the game of whack-a-mole with bot operators. If you’re not already using Cloudflare’s bot detection , check it out and establish the Trust ecosystem that works for you.
